etymologies.etymologyHTML: From flat +‎ -er (comparative suffix). Compare Icelandic flatari (“flatter, more flat”).

definitions.definition: comparative form of flat: more flat

etymologies.etymologyHTML: flatter (third-person singular simple present flatters, present participle flattering, simple past and past participle flattered) (transitive, intransitive)

definitions.definition: To compliment someone, often (but not necessarily) insincerely and sometimes to win favour.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 29:5:
quote.text: A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet.

quote.citation: 1855, William H. Prescott, History of the Reign of Philip the Second, King of Spain, Boston: Phillips, Sampson & Co., Volume 1, Book 1, Chapter 7, p. 242,[1]
quote.text: Some he complimented for their bravery; others he flattered by asking their advice.

definitions.definition: To enhance or gratify someone's vanity by praising them.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iv]:
quote.text: Here is her picture: let me see; I think,If I had such a tire, this face of mineWere full as lovely as is this of hers:And yet the painter flatter’d her a little  […]

definitions.definition: To encourage or cheer someone with (usually false) hope.

quote.citation: 1743, Robert Drury, The Pleasant, and Surprizing Adventures of Mr. Robert Drury, during his Fifteen Years Captivity on the Island of Madagascar‎[2], London, page 9:
quote.text: […]  I went up, and sat there two Hours and an half before I cou’d discern any Thing like Land; and when I first saw it I told my Comrade, but not being certain I wou’d not call out; for the Case was of such Importance, that they were not to be trifled with, or flatter’d into vain Hopes.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) In phrasal verb "to flatter with": to encourage, inspire with hope.

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Twelfe Night, or What You Will”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v], page 287, column 2:
quote.text: Run after that ſame peeuiſh Meſſenger / The Countes man: he left this Ring behinde him / Would I, or not: tell him, Ile none of it. / Deſire him not to flatter with his Lord, / Nor hold him vp with hopes, I am not for him:

definitions.definition: (usually reflexive) To cheer or please (with the idea that); congratulate oneself, especially when the perception is false.

quote.citation: 1593, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC‎[3]:
quote.text: The dire imagination she did followThis sound of hope doth labour to expel;For now reviving joy bids her rejoice,And flatters her it is Adonis’ voice.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From flat (“to make flat, flatten”) +‎ -er (agent suffix).

definitions.definition: A type of set tool used by blacksmiths.
A drawplate with a narrow, rectangular orifice, for drawing flat strips such as watch springs.
Someone who flattens, purposely or accidentally. Also flattener.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From flat (“dwelling, apartment”) +‎ -er (residency suffix).

definitions.definition: (British, New Zealand, slang) Someone who lives in a rented flat.
